question: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Rihards Kols (ECR), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Veronika Vrecionová (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Alexandr Vondra (ECR), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Matej Tonin (PPE) Subject:

In recent years, and particularly following the Hamas-led atrocities of 7 October 2023, a number of EU donor governments, including the Commission, have re-examined their funding of, and cooperation with, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) active in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. For example, in January 2026, Sweden reportedly stopped all taxpayer-funded grants to the aid organisation Islamic Relief Sweden, following concerns that individuals within the group may have links to anti-democratic or violent activities1. In 2025, the German Government reportedly defunded NGOs that denied Israel’s right to exist2. In January 2022, the Dutch Government announced that the Netherlands would cease all funding to the Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC)3. On 16 March 2026, the Commission announced EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance for the Middle East in 2026, including EUR 124 million allocated to the West Bank and Gaza and EUR 100 million to Lebanon4. In this context, and in the light of recent efforts by Member States to increase the accountability and responsibility of humanitarian aid provision, what steps is the Commission taking to update funding contracts, partner vetting and oversight mechanisms for NGOs, UN agencies and local implementing partners to ensure that the EU supports those actually furthering EU goals and does not reward entities characterised by antisemitic, antidemocratic, and/or violent activities and/or leadership?

answer: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Rihards Kols (ECR), Mieke Andriese (PfE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Veronika Vrecionová (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Ondřej Krutílek (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Elena Donazzan (ECR), Sander Smit (ECR), Alexandr Vondra (ECR), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Antonio López-Istúriz White (PPE), Stephen Nikola Bartulica (ECR), Matej Tonin (PPE) (14 April 2026) Subject: Re-examination of EU humanitarian funding to the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon In recent years, and particularly following the Hamas-led atrocities of 7 October 2023, a number of EU donor governments, including the Commission, have re-examined their funding of, and cooperation with, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) active in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. For example, in January 2026, Sweden reportedly stopped all taxpayer-funded grants to the aid organisation Islamic Relief Sweden, following concerns that individuals within the group may have links to anti-democratic or violent activities (1). In 2025, the German Government reportedly defunded NGOs that denied Israel’s right to exist (2). In January 2022, the Dutch Government announced that the Netherlands would cease all funding to the Union of Agricultural Work Committees (UAWC) (3). On 16 March 2026, the Commission announced EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance for the Middle East in 2026, including EUR 124 million allocated to the West Bank and Gaza and EUR 100 million to Lebanon (4). In this context, and in the light of recent efforts by Member States to increase the accountability and responsibility of humanitarian aid provision, what steps is the Commission taking to update funding contracts, partner vetting and oversight mechanisms for NGOs, UN agencies and local implementing partners to ensure that the EU supports those actually furthering EU goals and does not reward entities characterised by antisemitic, anti-democratic, and/or violent activities and/or leadership? (23 June 2026) The Commission is committed to ensuring that EU funding is allocated effectively and responsibly to defend the dignity of those in need in line with the values and goals of the EU. The Commission is aware of the complex operational context in which EU-funded entities operate in the occupied Palestinian territory (including in the Gaza Strip) and Lebanon. This is why robust safeguards are in place, covering due diligence and risk assessments (ex-ante checks), implementation monitoring, and post-funding oversight and controls (ex-post verification). The Commission’s non-governmental partners are thoroughly assessed against their capacity to observe basic principles and obligations, including respect of the relevant EU, international and national law, as well as compliance with transparency, accountability and internal controls, including risk management mechanisms. Under the regulation (EU) 2024/2509 (1), in line with Article 138, the Commission applies strict safeguards to ensure that a person or entity is excluded from EU funding if they are involved in any criminal activity, including terrorist financing and terrorist offences. As has always been the case, the Commission will ensure that funding allocations are made in accordance with the mechanisms outlined above in the context of the EUR 458 million in humanitarian assistance announced for the Middle East in 2026 (2).

In line with the Joint Communication on humanitarian action (3), the Commission reaffirms its commitment to remain a principled, reliable and predictable humanitarian partner, providing needs-based, inclusive and non-discriminatory assistance, while adapting its ways of working to maximise effectiveness and impact.
